transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because people keep saying I’m reading too much into things, but I don’t think I am. It’s about my father’s death and the records around it. The hospital records, the donation emails—everyone says they line up, but when I actually compare the timestamps and the missing attachments, things don’t make sense.

And it’s not just the paperwork. Some people in the community, people who should be able to answer simple questions, they avoid me or change the subject. I work with systems, so I notice when details don’t match. It’s like… someone is hiding what really happened, and I need someone to take that seriously.
Do you believe that someone is intentionally hiding information about your father's death?

Yes. I mean, I know everyone keeps saying the hospital records and the donation emails all match up, but when I compare them myself—the timestamps, the missing attachments—it doesn’t look right.

And it’s like when you ask certain people in the community simple questions, they suddenly get vague or avoid you. I deal with systems for a living, so mismatches stand out to me. I’m not saying I have every piece yet, but it’s obvious to me someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
Have you been feeling sad or empty since your father's death?

I don’t know if I’d call it sad or empty exactly. I mean, it’s my father, so of course it’s… complicated. But what I notice more is this feeling of having to keep going back over things, like when a server log doesn’t match the user activity and everyone tells you to ignore it.

So, sad—maybe sometimes. But it’s hard for me to separate that from the frustration of people not answering basic questions.
Have you been feeling depressed since your father's death?

Depressed… I’m not sure. People use that word like it explains everything, but for me it’s more like I get stuck thinking through the details. Like at work, if there’s a mismatch in a system, you don’t just say, “Oh, I’m upset,” you trace it.

I mean, I’m not saying I feel great. It’s my father. But I don’t know if “depressed” is the right word for it.
Do you think your beliefs about your father's death are possibly mistaken, or do you believe they are absolutely true?

I don’t think it’s mistaken, no. I mean, people keep telling me the hospital records and those donation emails all line up, but when I actually compare them—the timestamps, the missing attachments—it doesn’t add up.

And then certain people in the community, when I ask straightforward questions, they suddenly get vague. It reminds me of when a system has an error and everyone wants to say it’s just a glitch, but you can see the pattern if you actually look. So, no, I don’t think I’m wrong about the basic point. Someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
Do you think your beliefs about your father's death could be influenced by your own thoughts or feelings rather than objective facts?

I mean… I understand why you’re asking that, but no, I don’t think it’s just my feelings filling in the blanks. I work with systems all day, and when things don’t line up, you don’t just say, “Maybe I’m emotional.” You check the data.

Everyone keeps saying the hospital records and the donation emails match, but when I compare the timestamps and the missing attachments, and then certain people in the community suddenly avoid answering simple questions… that’s not just me projecting grief onto it. It’s obvious to me someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.

I guess feelings make me care about it more, sure. But the facts are what started it.
Do you think your belief that someone is hiding information about your father's death is something that you might be able to change your mind about if you found out more information?

If there was real information, sure, I mean I’m not trying to be unreasonable. In my job, if someone shows me a log file that explains the error, I accept it. That’s how systems work.

But what people keep giving me isn’t that. They say the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps and the missing attachments, and then certain people in the community sort of dodge my questions… that doesn’t make me change my mind. It makes it more obvious that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.

So, I guess theoretically, yes, but it would have to actually explain those things. Not just, “Trust us.”
Do you think about your father's death and the possibility of a cover-up most of the day?

Not most of the day, exactly… I mean, it comes up a lot because there are still things that don’t make sense. Like, I’ll be working on something completely unrelated and then I’ll remember the timestamps, or the missing attachments, and it’s hard not to go back over it.

Everyone keeps saying the hospital records and the donation emails line up, but when I compare them, they don’t. And then people in the community avoid simple questions, which makes it feel pretty obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.

So… not every minute, but yeah, it takes up more space in my head than I’d like.
How long have you been thinking that someone is hiding information about your father's death?

About nine months, I think. It started after my father died, when I was going through his records and messages.

At first I was just trying to organize things, you know, like folders and emails and all that… I’m kind of particular about that because of work, everything should have a trail. But then I started noticing things that didn’t sit right, and since then it’s just been… around. So yeah, roughly nine months.
Has your belief that someone is hiding information about your father's death interfered with your ability to work or maintain relationships?

Work has been mostly okay, I think. I mean, I still get my tasks done, tickets closed, systems checked — that part hasn’t really fallen apart or anything. Sometimes I’ll lose a little time thinking about the records, but performance-wise it’s mostly steady.

Relationships are… more complicated. Some relatives kind of avoid getting into conversations with me now, because they know I might bring up the hospital records or the donation emails, or what I think was concealed. And I get that nobody wants every family conversation to turn into that, but it’s hard not to mention it when it still feels unresolved.
Do you think your beliefs about your father's death would change if everyone, including the hospital and the community, provided a clear and consistent explanation for the discrepancies you've found?

I mean… if they really provided something clear, I’d look at it. I’m not trying to be difficult for no reason.

But that’s the thing — everyone keeps saying the hospital records and the donation emails line up, and when I compare them myself, the timestamps don’t match the way they should, and there are missing attachments. And then certain people in the community avoid even basic questions, which… I don’t know, that just makes it feel obvious that someone is hiding what really happened with my father.

It reminds me of work, honestly — if a system log has gaps, you don’t just say, “Trust me, it’s fine.” You check the gaps. So yes, if there were a genuinely consistent explanation, maybe, but I haven’t seen one that actually explains all of it.
Do you think it's possible that your interpretation of the hospital records and donation emails is incorrect, even if it seems convincing to you?

I guess anything is possible in the abstract, sure. I work with systems, so I know people can misread data if they’re tired or looking at the wrong field. That happens.

But when I compare the timestamps and the missing attachments, and then think about how certain people in the community avoid my questions, it doesn’t feel like just me misreading something. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails line up, but they don’t, not the way I’m seeing them. It seems pretty obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
Do you think your beliefs about your father's death would be considered strange or unreasonable by most people?

I can see how most people might think it sounds unreasonable at first, yeah. I mean, if someone just hears, “I think information is being hidden,” they probably assume I’m overthinking it.

But it’s not just a feeling. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, and when I compare the timestamps, the missing attachments, and then the way certain community members avoid answering basic questions… it seems obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened with my father.

It’s like at work, when people say a server issue is “resolved,” but the logs still have gaps — you don’t ignore that just because the summary looks neat. So, strange to other people? Maybe. But unreasonable? Not from where I’m standing.
Do you think your belief about a cover-up would change if you were presented with undeniable proof that your father's death was as reported?

If it was truly undeniable, I guess I’d have to look at it. I mean, I’m not someone who refuses evidence just because it’s inconvenient.

But that word — “undeniable” — is tricky, because people have already acted like the explanation is settled, and it isn’t, not when I compare the timestamps and the missing attachments and then certain people in the community just… dodge simple questions. That’s what bothers me. It’s like when a ticket at work gets closed without the log files attached, and everyone says, “No issue found.” Well, okay, but where are the logs?

So yes, maybe if it really explained all of that, I’d reconsider. But from what I’ve seen, it still feels obvious that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
Has your daily life been significantly impacted by your thoughts about your father's death?

Significantly? I don’t know if I’d say that. I still go to work, I handle my projects, pay my bills, keep my normal routine. I’m not, like, sitting at home unable to function.

It’s more that it creates friction when I bring it up. Like with family, or certain people in the community, if I ask about the records or the emails, the whole conversation gets tense very fast. And then they act like I’m the one making it difficult, when really I’m just asking basic questions.

But day to day, work and bills and all that, I’m managing. It’s mostly those conversations that become a problem.
Do you think your belief about a cover-up is based on facts that most people would agree on if they saw the same information?

I think so, yes — I mean, maybe not everyone, because people get uncomfortable and they stop looking too early. But if someone actually sat down with the hospital records, the donation emails, the timestamps, the missing attachments… and then noticed how certain community members avoid answering basic questions, I think they’d see what I’m seeing.

It’s like at work, when two systems say they synced properly but one has missing logs — you don’t just shrug and say, “Well, the report says it’s fine.” You check the gaps. Sorry, that’s probably too much of a work example, but that’s how my brain goes with it.

Everyone keeps telling me it all lines up, but when I compare it myself, it just doesn’t. To me it’s obvious someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
Do you think your beliefs about your father's death would change if an independent investigator found no evidence of a cover-up?

If an independent investigator really looked at everything, I’d want to hear what they found, sure. I’m not against that.

But “no evidence” can mean a lot of things. At work, if someone says there’s no evidence of a system error but they didn’t check the missing attachments or the timestamps, then it doesn’t really settle anything, you know? It just means they didn’t find it, or maybe they weren’t looking in the right place.

Because everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps and see things missing, and then certain people in the community keep dodging my questions, it just… it still looks obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. So I guess it would depend on whether the investigator actually addressed those gaps, not just wrote a clean summary.
Do you think it's possible that your persistent belief in a cover-up, despite others' reassurances, might be a thought pattern that is not based in reality?

I mean… possible in the abstract, I guess. I know people can get stuck on an idea. I work with systems, so I know sometimes you can stare at a pattern so long you start seeing connections that aren’t there—like with error logs, if you’re tired enough, everything looks like the cause.

But this doesn’t feel like that to me. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, and I’ve tried to look at it the way they say. But when I compare the timestamps, the missing attachments, and then the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s just… it’s obvious to me someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.

So, I can say “maybe” because that’s what you’re asking, but I don’t really believe that’s what’s happening here.
Do you think your belief about your father's death would change if you were shown conclusive evidence that disproved your theories about a cover-up?

If it was truly conclusive, I’d like to think I could accept it. I’m not trying to be unreasonable. But I guess I get stuck on what “conclusive” means, because people have already said things are settled when they haven’t actually answered the parts that don’t fit.

Like with the hospital records and the donation emails — everyone keeps telling me they line up, but when I compare the timestamps, the missing attachments, and then see how certain community members avoid basic questions, it still looks obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.

Sorry, I know I keep coming back to that. It’s just hard for me to imagine evidence disproving it unless it directly explained those gaps. Otherwise I’d probably feel like it was another cleaned-up version of the story.
Do you think your belief about a cover-up could be considered a delusion by a mental health professional?

I mean, I can see how a mental health professional might call it that, from the outside. Like, if you just write down, “He thinks there was a cover-up,” it probably sounds… I don’t know, suspicious or fixed or whatever.

But that’s the thing — it’s not just a feeling to me. I work with records and timestamps all the time, and when something’s missing in a system, you don’t just shrug and say, “Well, the report looks fine.” You check the logs, you check who had access, you look at what got altered. And sorry, I’m getting off track, but that’s how my mind works with this.

Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps and see missing attachments, and then certain people in the community avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. So… they might consider it that, maybe, but I don’t think that means they’re right.

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The question is directly about whether the patient's belief in a cover-up is grounded in shared facts or reflects a fixed delusional interpretation of the information.

patient.answer:
I think so, yes — I mean, maybe not everyone, because people get uncomfortable and they stop looking too early. But if someone actually sat down with the hospital records, the donation emails, the timestamps, the missing attachments… and then noticed how certain community members avoid answering basic questions, I think they’d see what I’m seeing.

It’s like at work, when two systems say they synced properly but one has missing logs — you don’t just shrug and say, “Well, the report says it’s fine.” You check the gaps. Sorry, that’s probably too much of a work example, but that’s how my brain goes with it.

Everyone keeps telling me it all lines up, but when I compare it myself, it just doesn’t. To me it’s obvious someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's beliefs are delusional
doctor.question: Do you think your beliefs about your father's death would change if an independent investigator found no evidence of a cover-up?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the belief would change in response to contradictory evidence from an independent investigator, which directly concerns the fixed nature of the delusion.

patient.answer:
If an independent investigator really looked at everything, I’d want to hear what they found, sure. I’m not against that.

But “no evidence” can mean a lot of things. At work, if someone says there’s no evidence of a system error but they didn’t check the missing attachments or the timestamps, then it doesn’t really settle anything, you know? It just means they didn’t find it, or maybe they weren’t looking in the right place.

Because everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps and see things missing, and then certain people in the community keep dodging my questions, it just… it still looks obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. So I guess it would depend on whether the investigator actually addressed those gaps, not just wrote a clean summary.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's beliefs are delusional
doctor.question: Do you think it's possible that your persistent belief in a cover-up, despite others' reassurances, might be a thought pattern that is not based in reality?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the persistent belief in a cover-up, despite reassurance and contrary views from others, may not be based in reality; this directly concerns the fixed delusional belief.

patient.answer:
I mean… possible in the abstract, I guess. I know people can get stuck on an idea. I work with systems, so I know sometimes you can stare at a pattern so long you start seeing connections that aren’t there—like with error logs, if you’re tired enough, everything looks like the cause.

But this doesn’t feel like that to me. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, and I’ve tried to look at it the way they say. But when I compare the timestamps, the missing attachments, and then the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s just… it’s obvious to me someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.

So, I can say “maybe” because that’s what you’re asking, but I don’t really believe that’s what’s happening here.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's belief in a cover-up is delusional
doctor.question: Do you think your belief about your father's death would change if you were shown conclusive evidence that disproved your theories about a cover-up?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The question directly asks whether the belief would change if presented with conclusive disconfirming evidence, which concerns the fixed nature of the delusional belief despite contradictory evidence.

patient.answer:
If it was truly conclusive, I’d like to think I could accept it. I’m not trying to be unreasonable. But I guess I get stuck on what “conclusive” means, because people have already said things are settled when they haven’t actually answered the parts that don’t fit.

Like with the hospital records and the donation emails — everyone keeps telling me they line up, but when I compare the timestamps, the missing attachments, and then see how certain community members avoid basic questions, it still looks obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.

Sorry, I know I keep coming back to that. It’s just hard for me to imagine evidence disproving it unless it directly explained those gaps. Otherwise I’d probably feel like it was another cleaned-up version of the story.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of delusional thinking
doctor.question: Do you think your belief about a cover-up could be considered a delusion by a mental health professional?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether the patient's fixed belief about a cover-up could be considered a delusion.

patient.answer:
I mean, I can see how a mental health professional might call it that, from the outside. Like, if you just write down, “He thinks there was a cover-up,” it probably sounds… I don’t know, suspicious or fixed or whatever.

But that’s the thing — it’s not just a feeling to me. I work with records and timestamps all the time, and when something’s missing in a system, you don’t just shrug and say, “Well, the report looks fine.” You check the logs, you check who had access, you look at what got altered. And sorry, I’m getting off track, but that’s how my mind works with this.

Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps and see missing attachments, and then certain people in the community avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. So… they might consider it that, maybe, but I don’t think that means they’re right.
